title: Surgical Reduction Techniques and Outcomes for Cervical Spondyloptosis: A Technical Report and Case Series.
paragraphs: Cervical spondyloptosis is a Grade V spondylolisthesis characterized by complete, greater than 100% translation of a vertebral body relative to its caudal counterpart. 1 This devastating injury leads to gross, multi-planar instability with complete disruption of all 3 spinal columns, including the anterior longitudinal ligament, intervertebral disc, and critically, the posterior ligamentous complex. 2 , 3 This uncommon injury, with fewer than 100 cases identified in systematic reviews, typically results from exceptionally high-energy trauma, such as motor vehicle collisions or significant falls. 4 , 5 Epidemiological data indicate a predilection for the lower cervical spine and cervicothoracic junction, with C6-C7 (30% of cases) and C7-T1 (38% of cases) being the most frequently affected levels. 5 The rarity of midcervical spondyloptosis is hypothesized to be an artifact of survivorship bias, as the catastrophic vascular and neurological damage associated with complete displacement at these higher levels is often incompatible with life. 6

Despite this profound structural failure, the clinical presentation of cervical spondyloptosis is marked by striking variability in neurological status. The spectrum ranges from complete tetraplegia [American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) Impairment Score A] to cases with no neurological deficits (ASIA E). 5 - 8 This clinical heterogeneity is explained by the “functional decompression” phenomenon, where the same high-energy force causing spondyloptosis also results in fractures of posterior elements such as the lamina or pedicles. 3 , 9 , 10 This shattering of the posterior spinal canal allows the spinal cord to drift dorsally, away from the site of maximal compression between vertebral bodies, thereby preserving neurological function. The existence of this neurologically intact subgroup fundamentally alters the risk-benefit calculus of management, as the primary goal shifts from stabilization for rehabilitation to preservation of existing function, making avoidance of iatrogenic injury a paramount concern.

The reduction techniques and stabilization approaches for cervical spondyloptosis remain controversial. 4 , 6 , 11 , 12 A global survey of treatment trends highlighted this variability, finding that while a combined anterior-posterior (360°) approach is the most common strategy (45%), anterior-only (31%) and posterior-only (25%) approaches are also frequently employed, with marked geographical differences in preference. 13 Our study provides detailed analysis of technical considerations and outcomes in a 2-patient series, providing comprehensive documentation of our surgical approach to offer practical guidance for spine surgeons confronted with these challenging cases.

This study presents a small series of 2 distinct cases of C7-T1 spondyloptosis (Figure 1 ) with differing neurological presentations and outcomes treated at our institution between January 2021 and December 2023. Inclusion criteria consisted of radiographically confirmed complete anterior-posterior displacement of adjacent cervical vertebral bodies after traumatic injury. Clinical data were collected from electronic medical records, including patient demographics, injury mechanism, neurological status (ASIA Impairment Scale), radiographic findings, operative details, and follow-up assessments. The study was approved by the Indiana University institutional review board, and patient consent was obtained for the use of clinical data and imaging.

Anatomic depiction of traumatic C7-T1 spondyloptosis. This illustration shows the preoperative injury, characterized by the complete anterior and inferior dislocation of the C7 vertebra with respect to T1. The image highlights the extreme instability and disruption of the spinal canal integrity at the cervicothoracic junction . © 2026 Christopher Brown, used with permission.

Comprehensive preoperative evaluation included detailed neurological examination using the ASIA Impairment Scale to quantify motor and sensory deficits. Radiographic assessment consisted of plain radiographs, computed tomography (CT) with multiplanar reconstruction, CT angiography to evaluate vertebral artery status, and MRI to assess spinal cord compression and associated soft tissue injuries. Particular attention was paid to the integrity of the anterior and posterior elements, the degree of displacement, the presence of associated fractures, and evidence of vertebral artery injury. Preoperative planning included consideration of reduction strategy, anticipated challenges in visualization (particularly for cervicothoracic junction cases), and determination of appropriate instrumentation levels based on injury pattern and bone quality.

In general, traumatic spondylolisthesis can be approached through an anterior only, posterior only, or anterior-posterior approach. Owing to the extreme subluxation of spondyloptosis cases, we recommend a combined anterior-posterior fusion and reduction technique in the following order. Complete reduction may be achieved at any of these steps depending on the degree of paraspinous soft tissue disruption, disc space disruption, and most importantly, facet fracture configuration posteriorly.

After positioning supine, the patient can be placed in Gardner Wells tongs with pin placement typically 1 cm above pinna in line with external auditory meatus. Next, we start at 10 lbs of traction and incrementally increase weight by 5 to 10 lbs (2.2 kg) until adequate or complete reduction is achieved, a maximum limit of 40 to 60 lbs is achieved, or undue changes in spinal alignment in other regions (eg, craniocervical junction) is seen. Of note, closed traction in the intensive care unit is generally not preferred for incomplete spinal cord injury due to the active cord compression that requires expeditious surgical reduction and decompression.

Following anterior cervical exposure to the prevertebral space, reduction can be achieved using manual manipulation of the affected vertebral bodies using a combination of simultaneous distraction and gentle vertical shear forces (Figure 2 ).

Following discectomy of the injury levels, a Cobb dissector can be inserted into the disc space as well to provide additional leverage at level of subluxation to distraction and reduce the malalignment (Figure 3 ).

Once anterior fusion is complete and patient is positioned prone, posterior column osteotomy at level of injury should be performed, which is usually already initiated by the original traumatic injury (eg, bilateral traumatic pedicle or facet fractures).

Pedicle screws immediately above and bilateral the disc space injury level are critical to allow adequate fixation strength and to use screw-head reduction devices to pull the cranial, anteriorly listhesed levels posteriorly into alignment (Figures 4 and 5 ).

Anterior reduction technique using caspar distraction pins. This image depicts a key step in the anterior approach to reduction. Caspar pins are placed into the C7 and T1 vertebral bodies. Controlled distraction applied to these pins helps to separate the collapsed disc space and realign the displaced vertebrae before performing the discectomy and fusion. © 2026 Christopher Brown, used with permission.

Anterior reduction technique using a Cobb dissector. This illustration demonstrates an alternative or complementary maneuver during the anterior surgery. A Cobb dissector or similar instrument is inserted into the C7-T1 interspace to be used as a lever, helping to lift the superior C7 vertebra and guide it into anatomic alignment with T1. © 2026 Christopher Brown, used with permission.

Anterior-posterior reduction and fixation technique. This image illustrates the anterior and posterior stages of the surgery. The key steps shown are: (1) First stage consisted of anterior cervical fusion and (2) second stage included placement of lateral mass or pedicle screws into the cervical and thoracic vertebrae. Contoured rods and reduction instruments are attached to the screws to apply corrective forces, pulling the spine into alignment before final tightening of the construct. A dissector is inserted to manipulate the facet joints during both stages.

Final 360° fusion construct for C7-T1 spondyloptosis. This illustration shows the final surgical result following the combined anterior and posterior approaches. The construct features an anterior interbody graft and locking plate at the C7-T1 level, supplemented by a posterior screw-and-rod system from C2 to T2. This circumferential (360°) fixation provides rigid stability, immobilizing the reduced spine to promote solid arthrodesis (fusion). © 2026 Christopher Brown, used with permission.

Postoperatively, patients were admitted to the intensive care unit with standard spinal precautions and fitted with a cervical-thoracic orthosis. Neurological examinations were performed daily to monitor changes in status. Upright radiographs were obtained within the first week postoperatively to assess alignment and hardware position, followed by CT imaging to evaluate the reduction and early fusion. Patient 1 had a preoperative vertebral artery injury identified on CT angiography that was managed with aspirin therapy based on vascular surgery consultation. Physical therapy and rehabilitation were initiated as soon as medically feasible. Follow-up evaluations were scheduled 1 month postoperatively, with radiographic assessment of fusion status and clinical evaluation of neurological recovery at each visit.

A 49-year-old woman presented with C7-T1 spondyloptosis after high-energy trauma from a motor vehicle crash. Her presentation was classified as ASIA C with incomplete motor deficits, exhibiting weakness in both upper and lower extremities with legs being particularly affected. Physical examination revealed intact cranial nerves, palpable step-off at C7 level, and variable motor weakness in extremities (Table 1 ).

Radiographic evaluation revealed complete anterior-posterior displacement at the C7-T1 level with posterior kinking of the spinal cord (Figure 6 A). The patient had an acute fracture of the right anterior arch of C2 with an associated short segment dissection of the right vertebral artery (Biffl 2A injury) (Figure 6 B and 6 C). In addition, there were bilateral pedicle fractures at C7 resulting in complete dissociation of the posterior element from the vertebral body and free floating C7 lamina and lateral masses. Cervical MRI demonstrated acute spondyloptosis with posterior kinking of the spinal cord and associated hematoma in the anterior and posterior epidural spaces from levels C7-T5, with a measured 5 mm override of C7 on T1 (Figure 6 D).

Preoperative imaging of patients 1 and 2. A , Sagittal CT scan of the cervicothoracic junction demonstrating complete anterior spondyloptosis (displacement) of the C7 vertebral body relative to T1 in Patient 1. B , CT angiography of Patient 1 revealing an associated short segment dissection of the right vertebral artery, classified as a Biffl 2A injury. C , CT angiography of Patient 1 zoomed in to better visualize the short segment dissection of the right vertebral artery. D , Sagittal short tau inversion recovery MRI of Patient 1 highlighting the severe spinal cord compression and posterior kinking resulting from the spondyloptosis, with a measured 5 mm override of C7 on T1. E , Sagittal and F , Axial view of CT angiography showing C7-T1 spondyloptosis and no vessel injury of Patient 2. G , Preoperative CT scan of Patient 2 displaying C7-T1 spondyloptosis. CT, computed tomography.

A 42-year-old man presented after a motor vehicle collision where he was an unrestrained passenger. His presentation was classified as ASIA A with complete motor and sensory deficits (Table 1 ). Radiographic evaluation demonstrated complete displacement at the C7-T1 level with spinal cord compression (Figure 6 E- 6 G).

Patient 1 underwent a staged anterior-posterior approach for C7-T1 spondyloptosis. Initial traction was deferred until the cervical spine was surgically exposed due to poor fluoroscopic visualization. Upon direct access, significant step-off at C7-T1 was noted. Traction was incrementally increased up to 40 lbs, and then, Casper pin manipulation was used achieving near-complete reduction. Discectomy was performed, followed by placement of a static interbody device and anterior cervical plate. The patient was then repositioned prone, and posterior fixation from C2 to T3 was performed using pedicle screws and lordotic rods. Intraoperatively, a completely free-floating C7 lamina was identified and resected, revealing an intact dura. Final alignment and hardware position were confirmed with O-arm imaging.

Patient 2 underwent a staged anterior-posterior approach for C7-T1 spondyloptosis. Initial supine traction using Gardner-Wells tongs reduced the deformity from grade 5 to grade 4. Surgical exposure revealed persistent step-off, and further reduction was attempted using Caspar distraction and a Cobb dissector, achieving partial correction to grade 3. Owing to facet fracture and joint impaction, further reduction was not possible anteriorly. A ventral dural tear was identified and repaired with Duragen and fibrin glue. A static interbody device and anterior plate with variable-angle screws were placed. The patient was then repositioned prone, and posterior instrumentation from C2 to T2 was placed. Bilateral resection of C7-T1 facets and decompression from C5-C7 were performed to address a dorsal epidural hematoma. Final reduction was achieved using cantilever beam technique via screw-head reduction towers, with excellent alignment confirmed by intraoperative O-arm.

Patient 1 was admitted to the intensive care unit with standard spinal precautions and placed in a cervical-thoracic orthosis brace. Her immediate postoperative examination showed diminished strength in all extremities. However, her neurological function gradually improved during hospitalization (Table 2 ). Upright radiographs and CT imaging obtained on postoperative days 3 and 4 demonstrated realignment of the spinal column and stability of the hardware (Figure 7 A). CT angiography repeated on postoperative day 7 showed a stable vertebral artery dissection, and she was placed on aspirin therapy.

Postoperative imaging of patients 1 and 2. A , Sagittal computed tomography of the anterior fixation from postoperative day 4 for Patient 1, showing the stable hardware construct and maintained alignment of the vertebral column. B , Lateral upright X-ray at the 1-month follow-up for Patient 1, redemonstrating maintained spinal alignment and the stability of the circumferential fusion construct. C , Postoperative computed tomography scan of Patient 2 redemonstrates severity of C7-T1 spondyloptosis with realignment postoperatively. D , Lateral upright X-ray of Patient 2 at the 1-month follow-up confirming integrity of fusion construct.

At the 3-month follow-up, most of her strength had improved, and repeat CT angiography showed stability of her Biffl injury, allowing discontinuation of aspirin therapy. By the 6-month follow-up, the patient had regained full strength in all muscle groups except for slightly diminished right grip strength (4+/5). Upright X-rays remained stable at 1, 3, and 6 months postoperatively (Figure 7 B), demonstrating appropriate alignment and progressive fusion. The patient continued to have some bilateral upper extremity pain at follow-up but was otherwise functional.

Patient 2 was discharged approximately 4 weeks postoperatively with tracheostomy in place. Immediate postoperative imaging showed stable hardware (Figure 7 C). At last follow-up (4 weeks), he showed no motor recovery and was likely still ASIA A, with sensation not assessed due to communication limitations from tracheostomy (Table 2 ) and stable upright X-ray (Figure 7 D). The patient was subsequently lost to follow-up with no further medical records available.

Our study demonstrates the variable and unpredictable nature of neurological outcomes in cervical spondyloptosis, despite appropriate surgical management with reduction and stabilization techniques. The management of 2 similar cases with distinctly different neurological presentations, Patient 2 with complete spinal cord injury vs Patient 1 with incomplete deficits, illustrates the variability of injury presentation. Although Patient 1 achieved excellent neurological recovery, Patient 2 demonstrated no motor improvement at short-term follow-up, highlighting that not all patients benefit from technically successful surgical intervention. This variable recovery pattern is consistent with systematic review findings that only 40% of patients with neurological deficits demonstrate improvement following surgery. 5 In general traumatic spine fractures that are unstable, neuromonitoring can be useful during closed traction reduction or during open reduction to detect early neurological injury. Patient 2 did not have neuromonitoring because they were ASIA A. In our experience, patients with severe neurological injury do not have anything to monitor and thus less likely to benefit. Patient 1 was ASIA C and had neuromonitoring during the procedure for somatosensory evoked potential and motor evoked potential.

Before surgical management, the surgeon must decide whether to attempt closed reduction through cranial traction. While this maneuver achieves success rates approaching 80% for many cervical fracture dislocations, its efficacy in complete spondyloptosis is significantly lower. 5 , 6 , 9 A comprehensive analysis of 66 cases found that traction achieved complete reduction in only 33% of patients, with partial reduction in 25% and failure in 37%. 5 The anatomic state of the facet joints is arguably the single most critical determinant of success. When the inferior articular facet of the superior vertebra becomes “perched” or locked anterior to the superior facet of the inferior vertebra, it creates a bony obstruction that traction alone often cannot overcome, even with substantial weight. 14

The choice of surgical approach for definitive stabilization is dictated by reduction outcomes and careful assessment of injury biomechanical characteristics, particularly posterior ligamentous complex integrity. 6 , 11 , 12 A posterior-only approach has emerged as a powerful alternative, particularly enabled by developments in cervical pedicle screw fixation. Unlike traditional lateral mass screws, pedicle screws provide true three-column fixation with superior biomechanical stability. 15 , 16 Several reports have documented successful treatment of C7-T1 spondyloptosis with posterior-only, short-segment fusion using cervical pedicle screws, challenging the traditional belief that all cases require anterior reconstruction. 17 , 18 A combined anterior-posterior approach remains the most common strategy, employed in 45% of cases and widely considered the gold standard for the most unstable injuries. 5 In addition, anterior access at the cervicothoracic junction (C7-T1) presents unique technical challenges. Exposure can especially be limited in patients with high thoracic inlets, short necks, or high body habitus. There is a misconception that these patients need to have sternotomy. However, we believe with multiple approaches and with traction that we can achieve enough reduction that a sternotomy is not needed for the anterior approach. Therefore, not all spondylolisthesis cases around C7-T1 need to be transferred to a tertiary center with thoracic surgery coverage. Nonetheless, these factors can complicate the anterior corridor and are important real-world considerations when planning approach strategy. In such scenarios, many surgeons may favor a posterior-only approach to avoid these anatomic constraints, even when anterior reconstruction is considered biomechanically optimal.

The contrasting outcomes between our 2 cases highlight an important underlying mechanism of injury. In Patient 1, bilateral pedicle fractures at C7 resulted in complete dissociation of the posterior elements from the vertebral body, creating a free-floating C7 lamina and lateral masses. This injury pattern effectively auto-decompressed the spinal cord, likely preventing further neurological damage. As a result, Patient 1, who presented with an ASIA C incomplete injury, progressed to nearly complete recovery by 6 months, demonstrating the potential for excellent functional outcomes when neural tissue remains intact. In stark contrast, Patient 2, who presented with ASIA A injury, showed no motor recovery at the 4-week follow-up and was subsequently lost to long-term care, illustrating the poor prognosis associated with complete spinal cord injury. This disparity aligns with established principles that incomplete spinal cord injuries have significantly better recovery potential than complete injuries, regardless of surgical technique employed. 5 , 8 Early surgery, ideally within 24 hours, is widely advocated to optimize recovery potential, although our experience suggests that the extent of initial neurological damage may be the primary determinant of outcome. 6 , 8

This study is limited by its small sample size, reflecting the rarity of cervical spondyloptosis, and the inherent limitations of a retrospective case series. While our cases offer valuable insight into surgical decision-making and outcomes, they may not be generalizable to all injury patterns or patient populations. In addition, 1 patient was lost to long-term follow-up, limiting our ability to assess sustained recovery or delayed complications.

Cervical spondyloptosis represents one of the most challenging cervical spine injuries, requiring individualized surgical planning. Our experience with 2 cases demonstrates that while technically successful reduction and stabilization can be achieved, neurological outcomes remain highly variable and largely dependent on initial injury severity. The anatomic state of facet joints emerged as the primary predictor of reduction success. Given the rarity and variable outcomes of these injuries, multi-institutional collaboration and honest reporting of both favorable and unfavorable results are essential to provide realistic expectations for patients and families.

Thank you to Chris Brown for the medical illustrations. Author contributions: All authors contributed to the study conception and design. Material preparation, data collection and analysis were performed by all authors. The first draft of the manuscript was written by BO-G, ASC, and GM and all authors commented on previous versions of the manuscript. All authors read and approved of the final manuscript.

Before surgical management, the surgeon must decide whether to attempt closed reduction through cranial traction. While this maneuver achieves success rates approaching 80% for many cervical fracture dislocations, its efficacy in complete spondyloptosis is significantly lower. 5 , 6 , 9 A comprehensive analysis of 66 cases found that traction achieved complete reduction in only 33% of patients, with partial reduction in 25% and failure in 37%. 5 The anatomic state of the facet joints is arguably the single most critical determinant of success. When the inferior articular facet of the superior vertebra becomes “perched” or locked anterior to the superior facet of the inferior vertebra, it creates a bony obstruction that traction alone often cannot overcome, even with substantial weight. 14

The choice of surgical approach for definitive stabilization is dictated by reduction outcomes and careful assessment of injury biomechanical characteristics, particularly posterior ligamentous complex integrity. 6 , 11 , 12 A posterior-only approach has emerged as a powerful alternative, particularly enabled by developments in cervical pedicle screw fixation. Unlike traditional lateral mass screws, pedicle screws provide true three-column fixation with superior biomechanical stability. 15 , 16 Several reports have documented successful treatment of C7-T1 spondyloptosis with posterior-only, short-segment fusion using cervical pedicle screws, challenging the traditional belief that all cases require anterior reconstruction. 17 , 18 A combined anterior-posterior approach remains the most common strategy, employed in 45% of cases and widely considered the gold standard for the most unstable injuries. 5 In addition, anterior access at the cervicothoracic junction (C7-T1) presents unique technical challenges. Exposure can especially be limited in patients with high thoracic inlets, short necks, or high body habitus. There is a misconception that these patients need to have sternotomy. However, we believe with multiple approaches and with traction that we can achieve enough reduction that a sternotomy is not needed for the anterior approach. Therefore, not all spondylolisthesis cases around C7-T1 need to be transferred to a tertiary center with thoracic surgery coverage. Nonetheless, these factors can complicate the anterior corridor and are important real-world considerations when planning approach strategy. In such scenarios, many surgeons may favor a posterior-only approach to avoid these anatomic constraints, even when anterior reconstruction is considered biomechanically optimal.

The contrasting outcomes between our 2 cases highlight an important underlying mechanism of injury. In Patient 1, bilateral pedicle fractures at C7 resulted in complete dissociation of the posterior elements from the vertebral body, creating a free-floating C7 lamina and lateral masses. This injury pattern effectively auto-decompressed the spinal cord, likely preventing further neurological damage. As a result, Patient 1, who presented with an ASIA C incomplete injury, progressed to nearly complete recovery by 6 months, demonstrating the potential for excellent functional outcomes when neural tissue remains intact. In stark contrast, Patient 2, who presented with ASIA A injury, showed no motor recovery at the 4-week follow-up and was subsequently lost to long-term care, illustrating the poor prognosis associated with complete spinal cord injury. This disparity aligns with established principles that incomplete spinal cord injuries have significantly better recovery potential than complete injuries, regardless of surgical technique employed. 5 , 8 Early surgery, ideally within 24 hours, is widely advocated to optimize recovery potential, although our experience suggests that the extent of initial neurological damage may be the primary determinant of outcome. 6 , 8

This study is limited by its small sample size, reflecting the rarity of cervical spondyloptosis, and the inherent limitations of a retrospective case series. While our cases offer valuable insight into surgical decision-making and outcomes, they may not be generalizable to all injury patterns or patient populations. In addition, 1 patient was lost to long-term follow-up, limiting our ability to assess sustained recovery or delayed complications.

Cervical spondyloptosis represents one of the most challenging cervical spine injuries, requiring individualized surgical planning. Our experience with 2 cases demonstrates that while technically successful reduction and stabilization can be achieved, neurological outcomes remain highly variable and largely dependent on initial injury severity. The anatomic state of facet joints emerged as the primary predictor of reduction success. Given the rarity and variable outcomes of these injuries, multi-institutional collaboration and honest reporting of both favorable and unfavorable results are essential to provide realistic expectations for patients and families.
